extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film viewers, and researchers interested in the 2004 short film Submission and its controversies (critics, students of film/religion/censorship).
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative criteria for assessing a controversial short film's artistic choices, political intent, ethical implications, originality, and social impact, as exemplified by the Wikipedia article on Submission (2004).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of women's abuse in accordance with fundamentalist Islamic law
rubrics_metrics.description: The film was praised for portraying the ways in which women are abused in accordance with fundamentalist Islamic law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how accurately and effectively the film depicts abuse tied to doctrinal interpretations; note techniques used (e.g., monologues, visual motifs such as Quranic verses painted on bodies) and whether these portrayals elucidate the claimed problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldness in questioning misogyny and culture of violence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Submission was bold in openly questioning misogyny and a culture of violence against women because of Koranic interpretations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the film raises important, difficult questions about religion and gender, and whether it confronts social norms or legal/religious interpretations in a way that stimulates debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness and depth of critique (avoid glibness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critic Dennis Lim: "It's depressing to think that this morsel of glib effrontery could pass as a serious critique of conservative Islam."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the film's argument is substantive and rigorous rather than merely provocative or superficial; examine evidence, nuance, and the strength of the film's critical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity and nuance of character portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: An unnamed critic referred to the stories told in the film as "simplistic, even caricatures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether characters are rounded and realistic or reduced to stereotypes; check for nuance in narrative and whether the film avoids caricature when dealing with sensitive subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoidance of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: After broadcast, claims of plagiarism were reported: Internet journalist Francisco van Jole said the duo had "aped" ideas of Iranian-American video artist Shirin Neshat (whose work used calligraphy projected onto bodies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate originality of concept and execution; compare to prior works that use similar techniques or imagery and note proper attribution or artistic distinction to avoid charges of copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation versus political pamphlet nature / artistic intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Director Theo van Gogh called the film a "political pamphlet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the film's stated or apparent intent: is it primarily artistic exploration, polemic, or political advocacy? Consider how intent shapes style, tone, and reception—and whether the film functions effectively within its chosen role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to offend and sensitivity to affected audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Writer Ayaan Hirsi Ali acknowledged that passages in the Quran depicted in the film could be seen as offensive, e.g., reading passages about a woman being slapped or raped being insulting to Muslim women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the likelihood and extent of offense to the communities depicted; consider whether the film's message justifies provocative choices and whether it offers sufficient context or critique to mitigate gratuitous insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of religious text imagery and ethical appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: The film highlights three Quranic verses by showing them painted on women's bodies (and uses the bodies as a canvas for verses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the ethical and artistic implications of using sacred texts as visual motifs on human bodies: consider respect for religious sensibilities, symbolism, artistic justification, and potential misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for real-world consequences and safety risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The film was linked to the assassination of director Theo van Gogh; a letter affixed to his body linked the murder to the film and its views regarding Islam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider possible real-world impacts of controversial content, including risks of incitement, threats to creators, and public safety; weigh freedom of expression against foreseeable harm and legal/security implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polarization of critical reception and public response
rubrics_metrics.description: The film "drew praise" for some aspects and "anger" for criticising Islamic canon; tens of thousands gathered to mourn Van Gogh after his murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how divisive the film is—measure balance of praise vs. condemnation in critical reviews and public reaction; consider whether polarizing responses indicate effectiveness or failure in communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of creator's prior reputation on reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Van Gogh was known as a controversial and provocative personality (described by a critic as a "radical-libertarian loudmouth").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account how a director/writer's public persona and history may color interpretations of the work and influence critical and public reactions; separate the work's merits from reputation-driven bias where possible.
